titre: A Croatian Earthquake, 41 Seismograms, and the Boundary Beneath Our Feet
accroche: On October 8, 1909, an earthquake shakes the Kupa Valley. Andrija Mohorovičić reads two sets of waves in it and deduces an internal boundary of the Earth.
contenu_vulgarise:
Geology textbooks call the boundary between the crust and the mantle the “Moho.” It owes its name to a single earthquake, and to the patience of the man who pored over it.

## An Earthquake at the Right Moment

Andrija Mohorovičić runs the meteorological observatory in Zagreb. He has had Wiechert seismographs installed there, the first in 1908, the second in 1909. On October 8, 1909, a strong earthquake strikes the Kupa Valley, a few tens of kilometers southeast of Zagreb. His brand-new instruments record it at close range.

## Asking All of Europe for Recordings

Mohorovičić does not stop at Zagreb. He writes to colleagues across Europe and gathers the seismograms from 41 stations. Comparing them, he notices a regularity. At stations less than 240 kilometers from the epicenter, one longitudinal wave and one transverse wave arrive. Between 240 and 720 kilometers, two of each arrive.

## Two Paths, So Two Layers

He concludes that the waves do not all follow the same path: some stay in the surface layer, others pass through a deeper layer where they travel faster, and overtake the first ones beyond a certain distance. There is therefore, beneath the surface, a discontinuity separating two media. He distinguishes phases that seismology now labels Pg, Sg, Pn, and Sn, along with numerous reflections within the crust.

## What “Longitudinal” and “Transverse” Mean

Longitudinal waves (P) make the rock vibrate in the direction of propagation; transverse waves (S) make it vibrate perpendicular to it. These are the two families of waves that leave an earthquake, and each has its two arrivals here. Finding two sets of waves of each family beyond 240 kilometers requires recordings from many stations, which only a network could provide. Mohorovičić thus sets out to demonstrate, from seismic waves, the existence of the discontinuity separating the crust from the mantle.

## A Publication Little Read at First

The work appears in 1910 in the annual report of the Zagreb observatory for 1909, in Croatian (56 pages), then in a German translation in the same volume. An English translation was not published until 1992, in *Geofizika*. The boundary has since received his name: the Mohorovičić discontinuity, abbreviated Moho.

The episode shows a method as much as a discovery: the Earth's internal structure is not read in a borehole, but in the comparison of recordings from forty-one stations.

repere.texte: After the Kupa Valley earthquake of October 8, 1909, Mohorovičić gathers the seismograms from 41 European stations: up to 240 km from the epicenter, one longitudinal wave and one transverse wave; from 240 to 720 km, two of each.
repere.source: Geotech d.o.o., Rijeka (geotech.hr), “Discovery of Mohorovičić's (Moho) Discontinuity”

carte.punch: The boundary between crust and mantle was read in the seismograms of 41 stations.
carte.idee: After the October 8, 1909 earthquake near Zagreb, Mohorovičić gathers the recordings from 41 European stations. Under 240 km, one longitudinal and one transverse wave; beyond, two of each: he deduces a discontinuity beneath the surface.

quiz.question: What does Mohorovičić observe in the seismograms from stations located between 240 and 720 km from the epicenter?
choix: A single transverse wave, the longitudinal waves having been absorbed
Two longitudinal waves and two transverse waves, instead of one of each
A single wave, slower than the one seen at nearby stations
No transverse wave at all, since they do not propagate at that distance
quiz.explication: Under 240 km, one longitudinal and one transverse wave arrive; between 240 and 720 km, two of each arrive. Mohorovičić deduces two different paths, and therefore a discontinuity between two layers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many stations provide seismograms to Mohorovičić?
choix: Just one, Zagreb's, which had recorded the earthquake at close range
Three, in Zagreb, Vienna, and Berlin, the closest to the epicenter
More than 400, gathered by an already organized international network
41, gathered by writing to colleagues across Europe
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mohorovičić asks colleagues across Europe to send him their recordings and receives them from 41 stations. It is the comparison among them that reveals the discontinuity.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which publication does his work first appear?
choix: In the Zagreb observatory's annual report for 1909, published in 1910
In an international geophysics journal, in English, as early as 1909
In a geology book published in Vienna in 1912
In the bulletin of an American academy of sciences
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text appears in Croatian (56 pages) in the Zagreb observatory's annual report, with a German translation in the same volume. The English translation does not arrive until 1992, in Geofizika.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the phases labeled Pg and Pn show?
choix: That the earthquake occurred in two successive shocks
That the seismographs of the time went out of adjustment under the vibrations
That the waves follow several paths, some within the crust, others deeper
That the longitudinal wave turns into a transverse wave at each station
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mohorovičić distinguishes phases that seismology labels Pg, Sg, Pn, and Sn. Their existence reflects different wave paths, and therefore a discontinuity in properties beneath the surface.
